about: Why your phone photos look better than real life. Factory #13, backlog row 14. Number hook, then one mechanism (stack dark frames, the grain cancels), then an escalation (night: up to 15) and Google's own words as the payoff. Nine is sourced twice: Apple's Sept 10, 2019 event on Deep Fusion (iPhone 11 Pro): 'It shoots nine images.' (Phil Schiller, transcribed by iMore; verify against Apple's event video), and Google's Night Sight post (Nov 14, 2018): on shutter press the Pixel camera 'sends the most recent 9 or 15 frames to our HDR+ or Super Res Zoom software'; it was already capturing 'As soon as you open the camera app'. HDR+ captures 'a rapid series of deliberately underexposed images' (Google, Apr 23, 2021), which keeps the sky from clipping to white at the cost of noisy shadows; merging the burst reduces noise (Hasinoff et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2016; Google 2018: 'averaging frames to reduce imaging noise'). Night Sight captures 'up to 15 if it is handheld' and 'makes them brighter than reality' (Google, Nov 14, 2018). Hero moment: line 'stack', nine grainy translucent sheets snap into alignment and the grain fades; the film's only coral stamp, 9 -> 1. Screenshot frame: lines 'night'-'reality', 1 FRAME vs 15 STACKED with Google's quote. Narration-led: record the voice first and key every visual beat to its word times.

lines.text: So why do phone photos look better than real life?
It starts shooting before you even tap.
Here's the trick. They're shot too dark, on purpose.
That keeps the bright sky from turning white.
But dark frames come out grainy.
So it stacks them. The grain mostly cancels out.
Grain changes every frame. The scene doesn't.
At night, a Pixel stacks up to 15.
lines.say: At night, a Pixel stacks up to fifteen.

lines.text: In Google's own words, brighter than reality.
Your photo isn't one moment. It's a blend.
Was your last photo real? Yes or no.
